name: SupportUtils
subcategory: shared inbox and help desk inside Gmail
tagline: Turn Gmail into a shared support desk with assignment, statuses, and analytics · no migration

pricing.notes: Chrome extension in early release; public pricing not yet posted at time of check. Treat per-seat as the expected model for a team tool.
pricing.freeTier: Free to install and try from the Chrome Web Store during the current beta.

verdictSummary: A rough version is a weekend project, but the thing that makes SupportUtils useful is the part that is hard to clone: it lives inside Gmail as a browser extension and keeps every teammate's view of a thread in sync in real time. You can hack a Gmail sidebar that stores statuses locally in an afternoon. Making assignment and status changes appear instantly on a colleague's screen, survive reloads, and stay consistent across a whole team is where the weekend runs out.
coreLoopDIY: Inject a panel into the Gmail thread view with a content script, let an agent set a status (open/pending/resolved) and an assignee on the current thread, and persist that per-thread state so it shows up the next time anyone on the team opens the same conversation.
requirements: a Manifest V3 browser extension with a Gmail content script
the Gmail thread ID and DOM injection points (undocumented and prone to change)
a hosted backend for shared per-thread state, not just localStorage
real-time sync so teammates see assignment/status changes live
auth scoped per organization so one team cannot see another's threads
Chrome Web Store review and ongoing publishing
whatYouLose: real-time multi-teammate sync of thread status and assignment
collision avoidance when two agents open the same thread
team analytics (response time, resolution rate, volume)
an extension that keeps working as Gmail's DOM shifts under it
onboarding with zero new UI because it is just Gmail
moatNotes: deep Gmail integration plus real-time team sync
replacementScope: single-user Gmail sidebar with local statuses
ongoingBurden: tracking Gmail DOM changes, real-time state sync, per-org auth, conflict resolution, Chrome Web Store review, and uptime for the sync backend
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay because the value is not the status dropdown, it is that a whole team can run support out of Gmail without learning a new tool and without messages falling through the cracks. The DIY build gets you a personal sidebar; the product gets you a synced, multi-agent inbox that survives Gmail changing its markup and a teammate resolving a ticket while you are still reading it. Keeping a Gmail extension alive against an interface you do not control is a standing tax most people would rather pay someone else to carry.

priorArt.name: Chatwoot
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source shared-inbox and support platform, though it replaces Gmail rather than living inside it.

alternatives.name: FreeScout
alternatives.desc: Email becomes an assigned team inbox with notes and collision warnings; you run it, and the nicer modules cost extra.

alternatives.name: Chatwoot
alternatives.desc: A proper support inbox with chat, email, and a help center; free software, billable server chores, and it lives outside Gmail.

alternatives.name: Zammad
alternatives.desc: A serious ticket desk with email, chat, SLAs, and a knowledge base; setup is the first ticket you will file.

alternatives.name: HubSpot Free Help Desk
alternatives.desc: A hosted shared inbox, live chat, and ticket queue for two users; assignment and analytics without touching a server.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Streak
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Also a Gmail extension, but it is a CRM/pipeline layer; shared-inbox assignment and support statuses are not its core job, so it misses the stated loop.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Google Groups collaborative inbox
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Free assignment and resolve/duplicate statuses on a shared address, but no real-time in-thread sync inside each agent's own Gmail and no analytics.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Freshdesk Free Program
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The no-cost program expires after six months, which is a trial with better manners, not an indefinite free alternative.

notes: Editorial comparison targets a single-user Gmail sidebar as the DIY substitute. The paid product's edge is the Gmail-native surface plus real-time team sync, neither of which the weekend build reaches. Extension is in early release; recheck pricing before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal, single-user substitute for SupportUtils: a Gmail sidebar that turns threads into trackable support tickets.
Use a Manifest V3 browser extension with TypeScript, React, and Vite; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: open a Gmail conversation, set a status (open, pending, resolved) and an assignee on that thread, and see those labels again every time the thread is opened.
Inject a content script into Gmail's thread view and read the stable thread identifier from the URL, not from brittle DOM text.
Store per-thread state (status, assignee, updated timestamp) in chrome.storage.local so it survives reloads.
Render a compact panel with the status control, an assignee field, and an internal note box, matching Gmail's own spacing so it does not look bolted on.
Add a simple local dashboard: counts by status and a list of open threads, read from the same store.
Handle Gmail navigating between threads without a full reload by watching history changes and re-rendering.
Put any config in an options page; ship no accounts, no server, no telemetry.
Write focused tests for the thread-id parser and the status store, plus one end-to-end pass that sets a status and reads it back.
Write a README covering install as an unpacked extension, the data location, and how to export the store as JSON.
Out of scope, and say so plainly in the README: real-time sync across teammates, per-organization auth, collision warnings when two agents open one thread, and team analytics. Those need a hosted backend and are exactly why a team would pay for SupportUtils instead of running this.
Expect Gmail's markup to change and leave a comment at every DOM assumption so the next fix is quick.
